extraction.name: BIG-Bench Hard (BBH)
extraction.description: A subset of 23 particularly challenging BIG-Bench tasks (27 subtasks) for which no prior result from Srivastava et al. (2022) has outperformed the average human-rater score.
extraction.creator: Mirac Suzgun, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, Jason Wei
extraction.citeAs: Suzgun, Mirac, Nathan Scales, Nathanael Schärli, Sebastian Gehrmann, Yi Tay, Hyung Won Chung, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Quoc V. Le, Ed H. Chi, Denny Zhou, and Jason Wei. "Challenging BIG-Bench tasks and whether chain-of-thought can solve them." arXiv:2210.09261v1, 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was curated from BIG-Bench by identifying tasks for which the highest reported model performances were below the average human-rater score, then filtering tasks using criteria on number of subtasks, minimum examples, presence of human-rater baselines, evaluation metric, prior model performance, and manual scope judgments. The authors manually inspected 36 remaining tasks and excluded 13 as extremely difficult or outside scope, leaving 23 tasks as BIG-Bench Hard.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper notes that BIG-Bench tasks vary in how clean their data and metadata are; some tasks added later in the curation process lack human baselines, and other tasks only have the minimum number of examples needed to qualify for submission.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data source is BIG-Bench, a collaborative benchmark with over 200 diverse text-based tasks. BBH is a curated subset of 23 tasks from BIG-Bench. For all but three tasks in BBH, the authors take a random subset of 250 evaluation examples; for Causal Judgement, Penguins in a Table, and Snarks, they use all available test examples in addition to three examples reserved for few-shot prompting.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors filtered BIG-Bench from 209 tasks down to 23 using explicit criteria: removing tasks with more than three subtasks, fewer than 103 examples, without human-rater baselines, or not using multiple-choice or exact match metrics; removing tasks where the best reported model beat the average human-rater; and removing extremely difficult tasks outside the scope of the work. They also randomly sampled 250 evaluation examples for most tasks.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For evaluation, the authors strengthened few-shot prompting by including both a task instruction and answer options in the prompt. They manually composed three chain-of-thought exemplars for each task in BBH and prepended "let's think step-by-step" to all CoT annotations in the few-shot exemplars. During evaluation they extracted the final answer based on keywords the language model is expected to produce ("the answer is") and measured exact match accuracy against ground-truth labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The authors manually wrote chain-of-thought exemplars for BBH and manually composed three chain-of-thought exemplars for each task. The benchmark also relies on human-rater baselines from BIG-Bench, where organizers enlisted a team of raters to manually solve each task and score them against golden labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper notes that human-rater scores are not representative of the entire population and should be interpreted with care. The human-evaluation component of BIG-Bench took almost a year, during which formatting and content of some tasks changed multiple times; raters solved a subsampled evaluation set, could use external resources such as the Internet, and some task descriptions were hard to follow. The authors also state that surpassing average human-rater performance should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that the authors make BBH publicly available and release the data and prompts used in the work, as well as the outputs from the Codex models, to facilitate further research.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Some tasks require knowledge about common practices and presuppositions in Western society; one multilingual task uses German source sentences and English translations.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors note they excluded Moral Permissibility because they did not want to delegate agency to models about moral judgement scenarios. They also caution that surpassing average human-rater performance on challenging tasks should not be confused with true language understanding or reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper states that some tasks require factual and general knowledge about the world as well as common practices and presuppositions in Western society. It also notes that human-rater scores are not representative of the entire population.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The benchmark is limited to 23 tasks selected through filtering and manual inspection. Thirteen tasks were excluded as extremely difficult, requiring domain-specific knowledge, impractical to solve within twenty minutes, ambiguous, or outside scope. Human-rater baselines should be interpreted with care because task formatting changed over time, raters used subsampled evaluation sets and external resources, and some task descriptions were hard to follow. The authors also note that language models still lag behind the best human-rater performance and that some tasks do not benefit from chain-of-thought prompting.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is an evaluation suite for measuring capabilities and limitations of large language models on challenging reasoning tasks. In this work it is used for few-shot evaluation under standard answer-only prompting and chain-of-thought prompting across PaLM, InstructGPT, and Codex models.
